text: Every Client Script you write runs in the user's browser, and ServiceNow hands it a global object called g_form, representing the form currently rendered on screen - the exact record the user has open, before anything is saved. This lesson covers the core g_form methods you'll use in almost every client script you ever write.

g_form.getValue of a field name returns that field's current value as a string. g_form.setValue writes a new value and updates what the user sees immediately - no server round trip, no database query. In this onLoad script, when category equals network, the assignment group field is set to Network Operations, purely in the browser. That's the core distinction from GlideRecord: GlideRecord touches the database on the server, g_form touches the form already rendered in front of the user.

Three methods reshape a field's behavior live, based on other values on the form. setMandatory toggles the red asterisk and the save-time requirement. setVisible shows or hides a field entirely. setReadOnly locks a field so it's visible but not editable. In this onChange script, when the watched field changes to the value one - meaning Critical - the justification field becomes both mandatory and visible; for any other value, it becomes neither.

Five methods make up the toolkit you'll reach for constantly: getValue and setValue for reading and writing without a server round trip, setMandatory for the red asterisk, setVisible for showing or hiding a field, setReadOnly for locking a field once it shouldn't change anymore, and addErrorMessage for explaining to the user exactly why a save is about to be blocked.

For the rare case where g_form's named methods aren't enough, getControl hands back the real HTML element behind a field, for direct styling or manipulation - here, tinting the short description field's background. Treat getControl as an escape hatch, not a first resort, since the named g_form methods keep working consistently across ServiceNow's different form renderers.

You now know how to read and write form values, reshape field behavior, message the user, and reach the raw DOM when you truly need to. Next up: the three real Client Script types - onLoad, onChange, and onSubmit - and the one with real teeth: returning false from onSubmit actually blocks the save.
